item.title: Why coffee tastes sweet without sugar
item.description:
Green coffee contains sucrose, glucose and fructose; the roasted bean and the cup contain almost none. Black coffee with no sugar added has no meaningful sugar, yet it can taste distinctly sweet.

Where the sugar goes: roasting drives the Maillard reaction and caramelisation, which consume sugars and convert them into hundreds of aromatic compounds. What is left is a trace of sugar-derived molecules — and with bitterness and acidity reduced around them, the brain reads those as sweetness.

item.title: USB WiFi adapters that show up as a CD-ROM
item.description:
A “multi-state” USB WiFi adapter carries on-board storage with a Windows driver, so on first plug it enumerates as a CD-ROM or flash drive. Windows autoruns the installer; other OSes see only a disk and no network interface, so the adapter must be told to switch.

Most mainstream distributions — Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian, OpenSUSE, Arch — ship usb-modeswitch with the adapter in its data files and switch silently; hand-switch only when the package is missing, the data predates the adapter, or the device is a rebadged clone.

item.title: DuckDB: SQLite for analytics, not a vector database
item.description:
An analytical database embedded like SQLite — no server, one file or in memory — but built for scans, aggregations and joins, not transactions: SQLite for analytics.

Where SQLite stores a row together, DuckDB stores each column separately:

1
2

row-oriented: [id=1, name=Alice, age=30] [id=2, name=Bob, age=25]
column-oriented: id: [1,2,3] name: [Alice,Bob,Carol] age: [30,25,40]

SELECT AVG(age) FROM users then reads one column, not every column of every row. It also executes vectorized — chunks of around 1024 rows, not one row at a time — using the CPU cache better and allowing SIMD.

item.title: Pausing and resuming a process
item.description:
The foreground job

Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP to the foreground job: frozen, memory and file descriptors kept open.

1
2
3
4
5

jobs # list suspended jobs and their numbers
fg # resume the most recent in the foreground
bg # resume it in the background
fg %2 # resume job 2
bg %2

Anything else

Find the PID, then signal:

1
2
3
4

ps aux | grep <process_name>
pidof <process_name>
sudo kill -STOP <PID> # or kill -SIGSTOP
sudo kill -CONT <PID> # or kill -SIGCONT

SIGSTOP cannot be caught or ignored — reliable when you do not control the process.

item.title: Atuin: shell history that syncs
item.description:
Atuin replaces shell history search: full-text and fuzzy search over a SQLite database rather than a flat history file, per-directory and per-session context, statistics, optional end-to-end encryption, and sync between machines. In zsh it replaces the default Ctrl+R reverse search.

Setup

1

eval "$(atuin init zsh)"

Near the end of .zshrc, then exec zsh.

fzf

fzf is optional (Atuin has its own fuzzy search) but still covers file finding, git branch switching, process selection, piped input. Atuin for history, fzf for everything else.

item.title: fd and plocate: live search versus an index
item.description:
fd is a filesystem walker, a modern find replacement: scans on demand, respects .gitignore by default, takes regex or glob patterns, executes per result.

1
2

fd config ~/.config
fd . ~/projects | fzf

plocate is a database-backed filename indexer, compatible with locate: queries a prebuilt index, never touches the disk.

1

plocate firefox

Trade-off: freshness for speed. fd sees the disk now — current, slow on large trees; plocate is near-instant but knows only what updatedb last indexed, usually via a systemd timer or cron.

item.title: Analytics basics: layers, parquet, similarity, clustering
item.description:
The factory

Analytics turns raw events — a click, an add-to-cart, a purchase, an approval — into trustworthy, queryable data:

1

Raw logs → Cleaned data → Business metrics → Dashboards

Databricks layer names, same progression:

Layer Holds Shape
Bronze raw files, as received append-only, untyped
Silver cleaned, joined, deduplicated typed tables
Gold business metrics aggregated, query-ready

CSV is the starting interchange format; Parquet is where it settles — columnar, compressed, typed, readable by DuckDB, Spark and Trino. A pipeline’s job is movement between layers; the tool is whichever engine does that without becoming maintenance.

item.title: Bash: scripting, expansion, and shell tricks
item.description:
Bash reference: interactive history tricks, a pure-bash scripting library based on pure-bash-bible, parameter expansion, and the shell’s weirder corners.

Interactive shell tricks

Create empty files without spawning touch — the colon is a no-op and redirection creates the file:

1
2
3

:> filename
>file
printf '' >file

History expansion

Syntax Effect
!! Repeat last command
!prefix Run last command starting with prefix
!$ Last argument of previous command
!#:1 First argument of current command line
!:1 First argument of previous command
^old^new Find and replace in previous command
  • !CD runs the last command that started with CD.
  • !$ reruns the previous command’s argument — reuse the path from an ls in another command: envm !$.
  • !#:1 references the first argument on the current line; !:1 the first argument of the previous command.
  • ^fuzzy^fzf corrects a typo or command name in the previous command in place.

Special parameters

  • $$ — PID of the current shell. echo $$.
  • $_ — last argument of the previous command. ls -la mydir, then echo $_ prints mydir.

Expansion and globs

1
2
3

mkdir -p mydir2/{dir1,dir2,dir3} # nested dirs in one command
rm file[14] # glob removal: file1 and file4
cp file.txt{,.back} # creates file.txt.back

Brace expansion covers numbers, characters, nesting, zero-padding, and steps:

item.title: A global gitignore for your own machine
item.description:
1
2

git config --global core.excludesfile ~/.gitignore_global
touch ~/.gitignore_global

Ignored in every repository on the machine: things about your environment, not the project:

1
2
3
4
5
6

.DS_Store # macOS
Thumbs.db # Windows
.vscode/ # VS Code
.idea/ # JetBrains
*.log
.env

A global ignore is personal, machine-wide, shared with no one. A repository’s .gitignore is committed and shared, describing what the project never wants tracked. Editor and OS junk goes global; project tooling’s output goes in the repo.

item.title: Find which process holds a port
item.description:
ss is the modern default, usually installed:

1

sudo ss -lptn 'sport = :3000'

1

LISTEN 0 128 *:3000 *:* users:(("node",pid=12345,fd=18))

1

sudo lsof -i :3000

netstat on older systems, from net-tools:

1

sudo netstat -tulpn | grep :3000

Killing the holder — a plain kill first, -9 only if it refuses:

1
2

sudo kill 12345
sudo fuser -k 3000/tcp

item.title: GNOME environment variables and login scripts
item.description:
Setting a variable without logging out

A modern GNOME session runs under systemd; GUI applications inherit that environment:

1
2

systemctl --user set-environment MY_VAR=value
dbus-update-activation-environment --systemd MY_VAR=value

The first sets it for systemd user services and later shell-launched applications; the second makes D-Bus-activated apps see it, how most GNOME apps start.

echo $MY_VAR prints nothing: variables are copied into a process at start, and your shell predates the change. Shell and systemd user session do not propagate:

item.title: SQL Anti-joins
item.description:
Rows with no match

Both find rows in TableA with no TableB counterpart:

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8

SELECT a.*
FROM TableA a
LEFT JOIN TableB b ON b.AId = a.Id
WHERE b.AId IS NULL;

SELECT a.*
FROM TableA a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM TableB b WHERE b.AId = a.Id);

NOT EXISTS is the better default:

Correctness with NULLs. LEFT JOIN breaks when the join condition is not exactly equivalent, with nullable columns, or when a joined-table filter lands in WHERE instead of ON — silently an inner join. Keep every joined-table filter inside ON:

item.title: Symlinked .desktop files, and why the window opens behind
item.description:
~/.local/share/applications follows symlinks: a .desktop file can live in dotfiles and be linked in:

1

ln -s ~/dotfiles/desktop/myapp.desktop ~/.local/share/applications/myapp.desktop

xdg-desktop-menu resolves the link, update-desktop-database indexes it, gtk-launch, rofi and dmenu find it. Mode 644, no execute bit:

1
2
3

chmod 644 myapp.desktop
update-desktop-database ~/.local/share/applications
gtk-launch myapp

A broken symlink makes the launcher vanish silently; Exec= paths resolve literally, not via the symlink.

Exec and $HOME

1

Exec=$HOME/scripts/open-browser.sh %u

Works on GNOME, KDE and XFCE, but the Desktop Entry specification does not guarantee it — a stricter launcher may not expand the variable. An absolute path always works:

item.title: Where HISTSIZE actually comes from
item.description:
HISTSIZE is interactive-only, so .zshenv is wrong — it runs for every shell, scripts included. It belongs in .zshrc; several files can set the value you see.

1
2
3

grep HISTSIZE ~/.zshrc
grep HISTSIZE ~/.oh-my-zsh/lib/history.zsh
grep HISTSIZE /etc/zsh*

Oh My Zsh keeps history settings in ~/.oh-my-zsh/lib/history.zsh, defaults above the 1000 that usually prompts the question; system-wide values come from /etc/zshrc, /etc/zprofile or /etc/zshenv.

Value and origin:

1
2
3

echo $HISTSIZE
echo $SAVEHIST
zsh -xv # every file sourced, in order

Change it in .zshrc, then source ~/.zshrc:

item.title: ZRAM compression: lzo-rle by default, lz4 for CPU
item.description:
ZRAM compresses memory pages in RAM instead of swapping to disk; the algorithm sets the trade between CPU time and memory saved.

The default on most modern distributions is lzo-rle: very fast, low CPU overhead, reasonable ratio. Confirm what is active — the bracketed entry is in use:

1

cat /sys/block/zram0/comp_algorithm

1

lzo [lzo-rle] lz4 lz4hc zstd
Algorithm CPU cost Speed Ratio
lz4 lowest very fast worst
lzo-rle low very fast medium
lzo low fast medium
zstd higher slower best
lz4hc high slow better than lz4

Pick lz4 when the CPU is weak or loaded and RAM is cheaper than cycles, lzo-rle for the default balance, zstd when memory is scarce and CPU is not.

item.title: Zsh completion: compinit, compdef, and custom commands
item.description:
Completion is function-based: on Tab zsh finds a completion function matching the command name, and it must exist. Zsh reads no --help.

Minimum setup:

compinit

zstyle ':completion:*' matcher-list 'm:{a-z}={A-Z}'

setopt AUTO_MENU
setopt COMPLETE_IN_WORD

compinit loads completion and builds a dump file, ~/.zcompdump. Rebuild it if changes do not appear, or zsh warns about an insecure completion directory:

item.title: Borg restore, partial loss, and silent exits
item.description:
Restoring

1
2
3

borg list /path/to/repo
borg list /path/to/repo::daily-2026-01-21 home/daniel
borg extract /path/to/repo::daily-2026-01-21 home/daniel/Documents

extract writes into the current directory and recreates the stored path — from /tmp/restore you get /tmp/restore/home/daniel/Documents, not an overwritten live tree. Listing a subpath confirms the path.

Finding a file

1
2

borg list /path/to/repo::archive-name | grep savegame
borg list /path/to/repo::archive-name --pattern '**/*filename*'

Across every archive, slow on a large repo but thorough:

1
2
3
4

for a in $(borg list /path/to/repo); do
 echo "== $a =="
 borg list /path/to/repo::$a | grep filename
done

Borg has no queryable index: searches read archive listings, so --pattern beats piping through grep.

item.title: Borg: what a backup contains, and what retention keeps
item.description:
What takes the space

borg list --format prints raw byte sizes by field: sort and tail to find heavy files:

1

borg list --format '{size:>12} {path}{NL}' ~/backup::desktop-2026-05-06 | sort -n | tail -50

1
2

1200000000 /home/user/videos/movie.mkv
420000000 /home/user/photos/raw.zip

numfmt --to=iec reads them as 1.2G, 850M, 420M; such findings usually mean a directory to exclude, not a Borg problem.

Verifying without restoring

1
2
3
4

borg check /path/to/repo
borg check user@host:/path/to/repo
borg check --verify-data /path/to/repo::archive-name
borg check --repository-only /path/to/repo

borg check verifies repository structure, metadata and archive consistency. --verify-data also reads and hashes contents — much slower, the only proof the data is intact. --repository-only limits the check to the repository, an archive argument to that archive.

item.title: Channeling: what the naked portafilter is telling you
item.description:
Channeling is water taking the path of least resistance through the puck: it finds a crack or loose patch and drives a channel through it instead of pushing evenly through the coffee. Parts of the puck get too much water and turn bitter, parts too little and stay sour. Both arrive at once — the signature.

A bottomless portafilter does not cause it. It removes the spouts that were hiding it.

item.title: Cloudflare Email Routing into Gmail, and the alerts it does not send
item.description:
Why forwarded mail lands in spam

Cloudflare Email Routing forwards mail from you@yourdomain.com to an inbox. As a forwarder it becomes the sender Gmail sees, so the original domain’s SPF and DKIM results stop matching the delivering server and Gmail defaults to suspicion. Records must be relaxed, not strict.

1

v=spf1 include:_spf.mx.cloudflare.net ~all

1

v=DMARC1; p=none; sp=none; aspf=r; adkim=r; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com

aspf=r and adkim=r stop a forwarded message being penalised for a check it cannot pass. p=none is the starting policy; quarantine or reject comes later, once delivery is stable.

item.title: Dialing in espresso: dose, yield, time
item.description:
“Dialing in” comes from the analog dial — the knobs on an old radio, later an espresso machine’s pressure gauge. It means tuning the variables until the shot tastes right.

The variables

Grind size is the most sensitive and the one you move; the rest are constants you hold still:

Variable Value
Dose (double basket) 17–18 g
Yield 36–40 g
Time 25–30 s
Ratio 1:2

A Gaggia Classic Pro with its stock non-pressurized 58 mm basket works at 18 g in, 36 g out. Brew temperature is the fifth variable, and without a PID it is not under your control.

item.title: Fingerprint login: PAM decides who gets asked
item.description:
fprintd owns the reader and answers authentication requests; the attempt count before password fallback is a parameter on the PAM module line that calls it.

Is the reader or the PAM stack the problem

1
2
3
4

fprintd-list "$USER"
fprintd-verify
systemctl status fprintd
lsusb

fprintd-verify success means the reader and stored prints are fine; the failure is the desktop’s PAM configuration. Fedora generates PAM files from profiles:

1
2
3

authselect current
authselect check
grep -R "pam_fprintd" /etc/pam.d/ /etc/authselect/ 2>/dev/null

That grep lists every service accepting a fingerprint, and by omission those that do not.

item.title: Honey and Black Honey: how much mucilage stays on the bean
item.description:
Green coffee is processed three ways: washed (fruit and mucilage stripped before drying), natural (dried whole inside the fruit), or honey — depulped, with some mucilage left on the bean through drying. Honey sits between washed and natural, and the colour name says how much sticky layer was kept.

Type Mucilage kept Cup
White Honey Little Cleaner, lighter body
Yellow Honey Some Sweet, balanced acidity, medium body
Red Honey More Sweet, syrupy mouthfeel
Black Honey ~100% Heavy, creamy, molasses and toffee

item.title: rclone: sync versus copy, deletions, and local encryption
item.description:
The one difference that matters

Command Copies new/changed Deletes on target
rclone copy source/ remote:target/ yes no
rclone sync source/ remote:target/ yes yes

sync mirrors the destination exactly: delete a save locally, run sync, and the remote copy goes too. Wrong default for backups — copy leaves anything the source no longer has.

Always preview a destructive run:

1

rclone sync /path/to/source remote:path/to/dest --dry-run -v

--delete-before changes when deletions happen relative to the transfer, not whether they happen. copy with --delete-excluded is the middle option when exclusions should also propagate.

item.title: What to back up on Arch, and a Borg command that does it
item.description:
/etc is 10–50 MB of mostly text: take the whole directory, not cherry-picked configs:

1
2

pacman -Qqe > ~/pkglist.txt # explicitly installed
pacman -Qqm > ~/aur-pkglist.txt # from the AUR

Those two lists make a rebuild an hour, not a weekend. Easy to forget beyond /etc: ~/.config, the shell dotfiles, ~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg, ~/.gitconfig, the bootloader config — /etc/default/grub for GRUB, /boot/loader/ for systemd-boot, outside /etc.

item.title: zsync: updating a big file over plain HTTP
item.description:
zsync delivers a new version of a file you already have. The server publishes a small .zsync sidecar of block checksums for the target file:

1
2

ubuntu.iso
ubuntu.iso.zsync

The client reads it, examines the local file, and fetches only changed blocks:

1

zsync http://example.com/ubuntu.iso.zsync

For a 4 GB ISO with 300 MB of changes, that is roughly 300 MB transferred instead of 4 GB.

At scale the key property: the server needs nothing special — an ordinary web server or CDN, and no copy of your old file:

item.title: inotify limits: instances, watches, and what a monorepo exhausts
item.description:
Two sysctls, two limits, both per user:

Setting Limits Default
fs.inotify.max_user_instances inotify instances one user may create 128
fs.inotify.max_user_watches watches one user may attach 8,192

An instance is one inotify_init() / inotify_init1() file descriptor — an fsnotify group, an event queue, the descriptor, and indexing structures for its watches. A watch is one attachment to an inode, bookkeeping linking watch, instance and inode.

Many tools opening listeners exhaust instances; few listeners over many files exhaust watches.

item.title: Reverting a protected branch with git restore
item.description:
develop and main are usually protected — no reset, no force-push — so undoing means new commits on top. git revert needs a commit range and a -m parent decision per merge commit: many chances to pick wrong.

1

git revert 4dbcaf5419d5b5aa19776d7ed733a163cacd95fe..dbffeb4da345fd0c66b0b7a8193a6582b409cd4a

The fallback is a second clone: target branch checked out elsewhere, everything but .git deleted, the good branch’s contents copied in, commit — works, miserable.

The one-liner

item.description:
On a branch drifted behind a busy main, git rebase origin/main conflicts on the first commit and again on each remaining one — 16 instead of one. Rebase an empty branch and replay the work as one uncommitted change.

1
2
3

git checkout branch-to-rebase
git fetch --all
git merge-base branch-to-rebase origin/main # last commit before the branch's own work

item.title: Git aliases: scopes, shell escapes, and the ones I use
item.description:
An alias is an ordinary config entry: it exists only in the scope where created (git log --graph --oneline → git graph), shell commands included.

Scope Applies to Config file
local the current repository .git/config (Windows: .git\config)
global the current user ~/.gitconfig (Windows: %USERPROFILE%\.gitconfig)
system every user on the machine /etc/gitconfig (Windows: %PROGRAMDATA%\Git\config)

Creating one

1
2

git config --global alias.c "checkout"
git config --global alias.ec "commit --allow-empty -m 'Empty commit'" # single quotes when the command has double quotes

Or under [alias] in the config file:

item.title: Git one-liners: prune, empty commits, show, grep, graph
item.description:
Each deletes a step: four commands, a branch switch, or a commit you did not mean.

Prune on fetch

--prune drops local refs to remote branches deleted upstream:

1

git fetch --prune

Stale refs accumulate with branch churn; git branch -a --contains <commit> gets verbose and slow.

Merge or rebase without checking out the target

A fetch already placed the remote’s refs locally as origin/…, and a branch is just a commit reference — no checkout, pull or checkout-back:
